adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Notes on migrating the reporting pipeline

For the better part of a year our team has been moving a set of nightly reporting jobs from a hand-written scheduler onto a managed orchestration service. On the whiteboard the change looked like a straight swap. In practice it touched almost every part of the system, and the parts that caused trouble were rarely the parts we had worried about. What follows is an attempt to record the reasoning while it is still fresh, partly for the next team that inherits the service and partly as a reminder to ourselves about how much of the work was invisible from the outside.

The first surprise was the inventory. Nobody could say how many jobs existed. The old scheduler had grown by accretion over seven years: a cron entry added by one analyst, a wrapper script left behind by another, and a handful of jobs that only ran when somebody remembered to press a button at the end of the quarter. We spent the better part of three weeks simply listing them and asking owners what each one was for. The final count was four hundred and twelve jobs, of which roughly a third had not completed successfully in more than a year. Several of those turned out to belong to people who had left the company, and two were writing files that nothing had read since the previous decade.

The second surprise was the dependency graph. The scheduler expressed dependencies only through timing, which is to say that a job started at two in the morning because the job it needed was expected to have finished by then. On good days that assumption held. On bad days the downstream job read a half-written table and produced a report that was quietly wrong. We built a small scanner that parsed the wrapper scripts and recorded every file each job read or wrote. That gave us a graph with far more edges than anyone expected, including a handful of cycles that had been harmless only because the jobs involved never ran concurrently.

Once the graph existed we could finally quantify the noise in the old system. The payoff came when we estimated the variance of the monthly totals: $$\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})^2$$ and we could compare the old and new pipelines on identical inputs for the first time. The old pipeline turned out to be noisier than the new one by a factor of three, but almost all of that difference came from one badly written aggregation job rather than from the scheduler itself.

The third surprise was cultural. People had built habits around the old scheduler. Reports were expected at particular times even when nobody read them until lunch, and several teams had written alerts that fired whenever a job finished late by even a few minutes. Replacing the scheduler meant replacing those habits, and that took longer than any of the technical work. We held a series of short sessions in which each team walked through its own jobs and decided what the new schedule should look like. The sessions were tedious and unexpectedly useful: twice we discovered that a job existed only to correct the output of another job that had already been fixed a year earlier.

Looking back, the migration was not difficult in any single step. It was difficult because the system had accumulated assumptions that nobody had written down, and because the only way to find them was to take the system apart and put it back together. The managed service is better than what we had, but the real gain is that we now know what we are running and why. The next migration, whenever it comes, should be easier for the same reason.

A short appendix of things we would do differently: start the inventory earlier, insist that every job has a named owner, instrument the wrapper scripts before touching the schedule, and resist the temptation to treat the dependency graph as a side project. None of these are novel observations. All of them were learned the hard way.
